title: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
summary: How sched_ext lets a BPF program decide which thread runs where: dispatch queues, the select_cpu, enqueue and dispatch cycle, weighted vtime in a few lines, and the watchdog that keeps it safe.
outcomes: Explain where the ext scheduling class sits among the kernel's classes and which tasks it takes over
Trace a waking task through select_cpu, enqueue, dispatch and the local, global and custom dispatch queues
Compute task weights and per-slice vtime charges and predict CPU shares under scx_simple
Explain how the verifier, callback checks, the watchdog and SysRq-S return a machine to the fair class
Choose between sched_ext schedulers and spot when one ignores nice or cgroup limits

lessons.title: Why the kernel lets a BPF program pick the next thread

blocks.md:
Every time a CPU finishes or preempts a thread, the kernel scheduler answers one question: which runnable thread goes next, on which CPU, for how long. On Linux that answer for ordinary threads comes from the fair class (CFS, now EEVDF), one general-purpose policy compiled into the kernel for every workload on every machine.

General purpose is the problem. A game wants low tail latency for its render thread, a VM host wants long uninterrupted runs for vCPUs, a server fleet wants a latency-critical service protected from batch jobs. Tuning knobs only go so far, and the policy itself is fixed.

The naive fix is to patch the scheduler. The sched_ext authors list why that is slow: the scheduler codebase takes newcomers a long time to learn, and every experiment means rebuild the kernel, reboot, rewarm the workload (they cite hours to warm memcache at Meta) and rerun. Rolling a new kernel across a fleet can take months. A bug in a patched scheduler can crash the machine.

**sched_ext** (the extensible scheduler class, merged in Linux 6.12) changes the deal: the policy is a set of BPF programs, loaded by running a user-space binary and removed by stopping it, with the kernel guaranteeing it can always fall back to the fair class.

Recall from the prerequisite courses: a *thread* (task) is the unit the scheduler places on a CPU, and BPF programs are verified and JIT-compiled before the kernel runs them. sched_ext uses a BPF feature called **struct_ops**: user space loads a table of BPF functions that fill in a kernel-defined struct of callbacks, here `struct sched_ext_ops`. The only mandatory field is `.name`; every callback is optional and has a default.

The kernel keeps several *scheduling classes* in strict priority order. On each pick it asks the highest class that has a runnable task.

blocks.title: Where sched_ext sits among the scheduling classes

scenes.caption: Classes are asked in this order on every pick. With no BPF scheduler loaded, the ext class is skipped and even tasks that set SCHED_EXT are run by the fair class as if they were SCHED_NORMAL.
A scheduler binary loads its sched_ext_ops. Without the SCX_OPS_SWITCH_PARTIAL flag, every SCHED_NORMAL, BATCH, IDLE and EXT task moves to sched_ext and the fair class is skipped entirely.
With SCX_OPS_SWITCH_PARTIAL set, only tasks that chose SCHED_EXT go to the BPF scheduler. The rest stay in fair, which sits above ext, so a runnable fair task always wins the CPU.

On an error, a stalled runnable task, SysRq-S, or the binary exiting, the kernel unloads the BPF scheduler and moves every task back to the fair class. Realtime and deadline tasks were never affected.

blocks.code:
# kernel built with CONFIG_SCHED_CLASS_EXT=y, BPF, BPF_JIT, DEBUG_INFO_BTF
cat /sys/kernel/sched_ext/state      # prints: disabled
sudo scx_simple &                    # load: runs the BPF scheduler
cat /sys/kernel/sched_ext/state      # prints: enabled
cat /sys/kernel/sched_ext/root/ops   # prints: simple
grep ext /proc/self/sched            # ext.enabled : 1
kill %1                              # unload: everyone returns to fair
blocks.caption: Switching a whole machine to a BPF scheduler and back, following the kernel docs. No reboot, no kernel rebuild.

blocks.md: sched_ext does not replace the scheduler core. It is one more scheduling class, below fair and above idle, whose *policy* (which task, which CPU, how long) is delegated to BPF callbacks while the core keeps the mechanism (run queues, context switches, preemption by higher classes).

Misconception: loading a BPF scheduler lets you control realtime or deadline threads. It cannot. Stop, deadline and realtime classes sit above ext and preempt it; sched_ext only takes over tasks that would otherwise be in the fair class.

blocks.question: A BPF scheduler is loaded with SCX_OPS_SWITCH_PARTIAL. On one CPU, a SCHED_NORMAL thread and a SCHED_EXT thread are both runnable. Which runs first?
options: The SCHED_EXT thread, because the BPF scheduler has been loaded and owns that CPU
The SCHED_NORMAL thread, because the fair class has higher precedence than ext
Whichever has the smaller virtual runtime, compared across both classes
Neither: mixing classes on one CPU makes the kernel abort the BPF scheduler
blocks.explain: Classes are consulted in strict order: stop, deadline, realtime, fair, ext, idle. In partial mode the fair class is still active and sits above ext, so its runnable task is picked first. Vruntime is never compared across classes.

blocks.question: Which problem does sched_ext mainly remove compared with patching CFS directly?
options: Scheduling decisions must be made in user space, which adds a context switch per pick
BPF programs run faster than compiled kernel C, so a fixed policy becomes cheaper
Each policy change needs a kernel rebuild, reboot, workload rewarm and fleet rollout, and a bug can crash the host
The fair class cannot run on machines with more than one L3 cache
blocks.explain: The motivation is iteration speed and safety: a policy is loaded and unloaded like a program, and the kernel can always revert to fair. BPF schedulers mostly run in the kernel (user space involvement is optional), and BPF is not faster than native kernel code.

lessons.title: Dispatch queues: how tasks travel from BPF to a CPU

blocks.md:
The scheduler core works per CPU: each CPU picks from its own run queue under its own lock. A BPF scheduler may want something else entirely: one global queue, one queue per L3 cache, a priority queue per cgroup. sched_ext bridges the two with **dispatch queues (DSQs)**.

A DSQ is a queue of tasks that can behave as a FIFO or, for DSQs the scheduler creates, as a priority queue ordered by a 64-bit *vtime* value. Three kinds exist:

- one **local DSQ** per CPU (`SCX_DSQ_LOCAL`): the only place a CPU ever runs a task from,
- one **global DSQ** (`SCX_DSQ_GLOBAL`), a FIFO shared by all CPUs,
- any number of **custom DSQs** created with `scx_bpf_create_dsq()`.

Vocabulary from the kernel docs: a task is **inserted** into a DSQ (`scx_bpf_dsq_insert()` for FIFO order, `scx_bpf_dsq_insert_vtime()` for priority order), and a task sitting in a non-local DSQ is **moved** to a CPU's local DSQ (`scx_bpf_dsq_move_to_local()`). Linux 6.12 called these `scx_bpf_dispatch()` and `scx_bpf_consume()`; the names changed later, which is typical: sched_ext gives no API stability promise to BPF schedulers.

When a CPU needs its next task, the rule is fixed: take the head of its local DSQ; if empty, move one from the global DSQ; if that is empty too, call the BPF scheduler's `ops.dispatch()` and let it fill the local DSQ.

blocks.title: Two CPUs picking work from local, global and custom DSQs

scenes.caption: Starting state. CPU0 has two tasks in its local DSQ. The BPF scheduler has inserted T3, T4, T5 into custom DSQ 0 (created with scx_bpf_create_dsq). CPU1 has just gone free.
CPU1 looks at its local DSQ (empty), then the global DSQ (empty). Only now does the core call ops.dispatch(cpu=1) on the BPF scheduler.
ops.dispatch calls scx_bpf_dsq_move_to_local(0). T3 moves from custom DSQ 0 into CPU1's local DSQ, and CPU1 runs it.
A new task T6 wakes up and the scheduler's ops.enqueue inserts it into SCX_DSQ_GLOBAL, the built-in shared FIFO.
CPU1 is free again. Its local DSQ is empty, so it takes T6 from the global DSQ. ops.dispatch is not called, so T4 keeps waiting even though it has been queued longer.
CPU0 always drains its own local DSQ first: T1 runs, then T2, before CPU0 would ever look at global or custom DSQs. Whatever lands in a local DSQ is committed to that CPU.

blocks.prompt: A scheduler only ever calls scx_bpf_dsq_insert() with SCX_DSQ_GLOBAL or SCX_DSQ_LOCAL from its enqueue callback. Does it need an ops.dispatch() callback at all?
blocks.reveal: No. Tasks never wait inside the BPF scheduler: they are already in the global or a local DSQ, and the core consumes both automatically before it would call `ops.dispatch()`. The kernel docs say exactly this, and the default `ops.enqueue()` (insert into `SCX_DSQ_GLOBAL`) is why a scheduler with only a name already works. You need `ops.dispatch()` once you park tasks in custom DSQs or in BPF maps.

blocks.md: DSQ ids are 64-bit values. Bit 63 (`SCX_DSQ_FLAG_BUILTIN`) marks the built-in queues, so custom DSQ ids must be below $2^{63}$. Bit 62 marks `SCX_DSQ_LOCAL_ON`, and the low 32 bits then carry a CPU number, which lets a scheduler running on one CPU insert straight into another CPU's local DSQ. Values computed from `include/linux/sched/ext.h`:

blocks.code:
SCX_DSQ_FLAG_BUILTIN = 1 << 63
SCX_DSQ_FLAG_LOCAL_ON = 1 << 62
SCX_DSQ_GLOBAL   = BUILTIN | 1         = 0x8000000000000001
SCX_DSQ_LOCAL    = BUILTIN | 2         = 0x8000000000000002
SCX_DSQ_LOCAL_ON | 3 (CPU 3's local)   = 0xc000000000000003
largest custom DSQ id = 2^63 - 1        = 0x7fffffffffffffff
blocks.caption: DSQ id layout. Custom ids such as 0 used by scx_simple never collide with built-in ones.

blocks.md: The two built-in DSQ types are FIFOs only. To order tasks by vtime you must create a custom DSQ and use `scx_bpf_dsq_insert_vtime()` on it; the kernel rejects vtime insertion into `SCX_DSQ_LOCAL` or `SCX_DSQ_GLOBAL`. This is why `scx_simple` creates DSQ 0 in its `init` callback instead of using the global DSQ.
A CPU only ever runs tasks from its own local DSQ. Everything else (global DSQ, custom DSQs, BPF maps) is staging. The pick order is local, then global, then `ops.dispatch()`.

Inserting a task into a local DSQ is a commitment. Once there, it waits for that CPU even if another CPU goes idle a microsecond later. Schedulers that want work sharing keep tasks in a shared custom DSQ and move them to a local DSQ only when a CPU asks via `ops.dispatch()`.

blocks.question: CPU2's local DSQ is empty. The global DSQ holds task X (queued 1 ms ago) and custom DSQ 7 holds task Y (queued 50 ms ago). Which task does CPU2 run next, assuming no new insertions?
options: Y, because it has waited longer and DSQs are served oldest first across queues
X, because the global DSQ is consumed before ops.dispatch() is ever called
Y, because custom DSQs have priority over built-in ones
Neither until ops.dispatch() chooses between them
blocks.explain: The pick order is fixed: local DSQ, then global DSQ, then ops.dispatch(). X is taken from the global DSQ without consulting the BPF scheduler. Y only moves if ops.dispatch() later calls scx_bpf_dsq_move_to_local(7).

blocks.question: Your enqueue callback calls scx_bpf_dsq_insert_vtime(p, SCX_DSQ_GLOBAL, slice, vtime, flags). What happens?
options: Tasks are kept in vtime order inside the global DSQ
The vtime is ignored and the task is appended FIFO
It is an error: built-in DSQs do not support priority-queue insertion, so you need a custom DSQ
The task is silently moved to the caller CPU's local DSQ
blocks.explain: Built-in DSQs (local and global) are FIFO only. The docs and scx_simple's comments say vtime insertion needs a DSQ created with scx_bpf_create_dsq(); invalid use is reported as a scheduler error, which unloads it.

lessons.title: The scheduling cycle: select_cpu, enqueue, dispatch, run

blocks.md:
A BPF scheduler is a set of callbacks the core invokes at specific moments in a task's life. The ones that make decisions for a waking task are:

1. `ops.select_cpu(p, prev_cpu, wake_flags)`: pick a CPU for a waking task. It is a *hint*, and choosing an idle CPU also wakes that CPU up.
2. `ops.enqueue(p, enq_flags)`: the task is runnable; insert it into a DSQ or keep it in BPF data structures (a map, a list).
3. `ops.dispatch(cpu, prev)`: a CPU has nothing in its local or the global DSQ; fill its local DSQ.

Around them sit notification callbacks: `runnable`, `running` (task starts on a CPU), `tick` (every 1/HZ while running), `stopping` (task leaves the CPU), `quiescent` (task stops being runnable), plus per-task `init_task`, `enable`, `disable`, `exit_task`.

Each insertion carries a **slice**, the time budget in nanoseconds the task may run before the core asks the scheduler again. The kernel's default `SCX_SLICE_DFL` is 20 ms. While the task runs, the core decrements `p->scx.slice`; at zero the task is descheduled. If a scheduler forgets to set a slice, the core refills it with `SCX_SLICE_DFL` and counts it in the `SCX_EV_REFILL_SLICE_DFL` event.

Here is a waking task on a busy machine, following `scx_simple`, the kernel's minimal example scheduler that keeps every task in one shared vtime-ordered custom DSQ.

blocks.title: One wakeup through scx_simple when no CPU is idle

scenes.caption: Task p wakes. The core first asks select_cpu. The default helper finds no idle CPU, so the callback just returns a hint and inserts nothing.
Because select_cpu did not insert p, the core calls enqueue. scx_simple inserts p into its shared DSQ, ordered by p's vtime, with a 20 ms slice.
CPU 2's current task stops. Its local DSQ and the global DSQ are empty, so the core calls dispatch for CPU 2.
dispatch moves the lowest-vtime task from DSQ 0 into CPU 2's local DSQ. Here that is p. The CPU it actually runs on is decided now, not at select_cpu time.
p starts. running() lets scx_simple advance its global vtime_now. The timer tick keeps charging p's slice.
When the slice hits zero (or p blocks), stopping() fires and scx_simple charges p's vtime by the time used, scaled by weight. Next lesson computes that charge.

blocks.prompt: Now suppose select_cpu finds CPU 5 idle and calls scx_bpf_dsq_insert(p, SCX_DSQ_LOCAL, ...). Which callbacks from the diagram above are skipped?
blocks.reveal: Both `ops.enqueue()` and `ops.dispatch()`. Inserting directly from `select_cpu` skips enqueue, and `SCX_DSQ_LOCAL` from select_cpu means the local DSQ of the CPU it returns (CPU 5), so CPU 5, which was just woken, finds p already in its local DSQ. This fast path is exactly what the kernel's default `select_cpu` does, and `scx_simple` counts it as its `local` statistic.

blocks.title: scx_simple's decision callbacks, traced for one wakeup

scenes.caption: p wakes with prev_cpu 2. The default idle-CPU search runs inside the kernel and reports no idle CPU.
Nothing was inserted, so 2 is returned as a hint and the core goes on to call enqueue.
enqueue reads p's vtime. p slept a long time, so its vtime is far behind the global vtime_now. Numbers in ms for readability.
The clamp limits sleeper credit to one slice: vtime becomes 10000 - 20 = 9980, then p is inserted into the shared DSQ.
Later a CPU finds its local and global DSQs empty. dispatch moves the head of the shared DSQ (lowest vtime) to that CPU.
When p starts running, vtime_now only moves forward: it is already 10000, so it stays 10000.
p used its whole slice (scx.slice is 0). With weight 100 (nice 0) the charge is 20 x 100/100 = 20, so p's vtime becomes 10000.

blocks.md: Where a task finally runs is decided when it lands in a local DSQ, usually inside `ops.dispatch()` on the CPU that is asking for work. `select_cpu` is an optimization: matching the final CPU saves a bit of work, and picking an idle CPU wakes it up.

Stashing a task in a BPF map from `select_cpu` does not skip `enqueue`; only a DSQ insertion does. The docs call storing tasks from `select_cpu` racy and discouraged. Also, the core ignores an invalid CPU choice such as one outside the task's allowed cpumask.

blocks.question: Your scheduler's select_cpu always returns CPU 0 for every task but never inserts anything. Your enqueue puts every task in one shared custom DSQ, and dispatch moves from it. Where do tasks actually run?
options: On whichever CPU calls dispatch and moves them to its local DSQ, so across all CPUs
Only on CPU 0, because select_cpu pins the task there
On CPU 0 for the first slice, then anywhere
The core rejects the scheduler for returning the same CPU every time
blocks.explain: select_cpu's return value is a non-binding hint (and the CPU it wakes if idle). Without an insertion there, the task goes through enqueue into the shared DSQ, and any CPU running dispatch can move it to its own local DSQ.

blocks.question: A task is in your custom DSQ and your scheduler never implemented ops.dispatch(). The local and global DSQs on every CPU stay empty. What happens to the task?
options: The core consumes custom DSQs automatically after the global DSQ
It waits forever, so the watchdog eventually declares a stall and unloads the scheduler
The task is promoted to the global DSQ after one SCX_SLICE_DFL
The kernel calls the default dispatch, which drains all custom DSQs
blocks.explain: Only local and global DSQs are consumed automatically. Tasks in custom DSQs move only when ops.dispatch() (or another callback) moves them. A runnable task that never runs trips the watchdog, covered in the last lesson.

lessons.title: Worked example: weighted vtime fairness in a few lines of BPF

blocks.md:
`scx_simple` gets proportional fairness from one number per task, `p->scx.dsq_vtime`, and one rule: the shared DSQ is ordered by vtime, smallest first. A task that runs gets charged vtime; a task with a higher weight is charged less for the same CPU time, so it comes back to the front sooner.

Weights come from nice values. The core converts the fair class's nice table (nice 0 is 1024) to the cgroup scale where the default is 100, so `p->scx.weight` lies in 1 to 10000.

blocks.caption: Left: sched_weight_to_cgroup() in kernel/sched/sched.h. Right: scx_simple's charge in stopping(), via scale_by_task_weight_inverse().

blocks.md:
Computed from the kernel's `sched_prio_to_weight` table: nice 0 gives $1024 \to 100$, nice -5 gives $3121 \to 305$, nice 5 gives $335 \to 33$, nice -10 gives $9548 \to 932$.

Now two CPU-bound tasks share one CPU: **A** at nice 0 ($w=100$) and **B** at nice -5 ($w=305$). Both start at vtime 0 and always use the full 20 ms slice. A full slice costs A $20 \times 100/100 = 20$ ms of vtime and B $20 \times 100/305 = 6.557$ ms. The figures below use an idealized model: every pick compares all runnable tasks, including the one whose slice just ended, and ties go to the task queued first.

Caveat: real scx_simple runs `ops.dispatch()` before the task whose slice ended is re-enqueued (the kernel passes it as `prev`), and its dispatch ignores `prev`. With exactly two tasks on one CPU it therefore alternates them 50/50; weights only bite when more tasks compete. Schedulers that want the ideal behavior compare `prev` with the DSQ head in dispatch.

blocks.title: One CPU, two tasks, vtime-ordered picks (v = vtime in ms at pick)

scenes.caption: Both tasks have vtime 0; A was queued first, so A runs 0 to 20 ms. stopping() charges it 20 ms, so A's vtime is now 20.
B has vtime 0 < 20, so B runs. Its charge is only 6.557 ms because its weight is 305.
B's vtime climbs 6.557, 13.115, 19.672: still below A's 20, so B keeps winning picks through 100 ms.
After its fourth slice B is at 26.23, above A's 20. A runs once and jumps to 40.
The pattern repeats: three B slices, then A. After 200 ms A has run 60 ms and B 140 ms. Idealized model: one CPU, no sleeps, and the task whose slice ended competes in the next pick.

blocks.title: CPU share: first 200 ms versus the long-run weight ratio

scenes.caption: Measured over the 10 slices above: 30% for A, 70% for B. Whole 20 ms slices make short windows lumpy.
Over a long run the shares converge to the weight ratio: 100/405 = 24.7% for A and 305/405 = 75.3% for B.

blocks.title: Long-run share of task B against a nice-0 task

scenes.caption: Against a nice-0 task (weight 100), each 5-step nice change moves B's share a lot: from 24.8% at nice 5 to 75.3% at nice -5.
Raise A's weight to 305 (nice -5): B now needs weight 305 just to get half. Shares depend only on the weight ratio.

blocks.prompt: Task C slept for 10 s. Meanwhile vtime_now advanced from 0 to 10000 ms. C wakes with dsq_vtime 0 next to a CPU-bound nice-0 task D at vtime 10000. Without the clamp in enqueue, how long would D wait?
blocks.reveal: About 10 s. C's vtime would be 10000 ms behind, and each 20 ms slice only adds 20 ms of vtime, so C wins 500 picks in a row before catching up with D. That is the classic sleeper problem. scx_simple clamps C's vtime to `vtime_now - SCX_SLICE_DFL` = 9980, so C is at most one slice ahead and D waits only one 20 ms slice.

blocks.title: Sleeper credit with and without scx_simple's clamp

scenes.caption: Unclamped: C wakes 10000 ms of vtime behind D and would monopolize the CPU for about 10 s.
Clamped in enqueue to vtime_now - 20 ms: C is only 20 ms ahead, gets one slice of priority, then the two alternate.

blocks.md: Weighted fairness in sched_ext can be three lines: order a custom DSQ by vtime, charge `used x 100 / weight` in `stopping`, and cap how far behind a waking task's vtime may be. Everything else (CPU placement, preemption, latency boosts) is extra policy you choose to add.

scx_simple charges `SCX_SLICE_DFL - p->scx.slice`. Its own comment warns that a task that yields has its slice zeroed and so is charged a full slice. Precise schedulers take explicit timestamps in `running` and `stopping` instead.

blocks.question: Under the idealized model of this lesson (each pick compares all runnable tasks), two CPU-bound tasks share a CPU: one at nice 0 (weight 100), one at nice 5 (weight 33). Roughly what fraction of the CPU does the nice-5 task get in the long run?
options: About 50%, because each task is charged the same vtime per slice
About 33%
About 25%
About 10%
blocks.explain: Shares follow the weight ratio: 33 / (100 + 33) = 24.8%, so about a quarter. The nice-5 task is charged 100/33 (about 3x) more vtime per millisecond, so it is picked about a third as often.

blocks.question: You remove the clamp from scx_simple's enqueue. Which symptom appears first?
options: CPU-bound tasks starve each other in a round-robin cycle
A task waking from a long sleep runs back to back for about as long as it slept, starving CPU-bound tasks
The verifier rejects the program because vtime can underflow
Nice values stop having any effect
blocks.explain: A sleeper's vtime stays where it was, while running tasks keep advancing. Without the cap, the waker is far behind and wins every pick until it catches up. If that exceeds the watchdog timeout, the scheduler could even be unloaded for stalling others.

lessons.title: Safety net, failure modes and schedulers in production

blocks.md:
The BPF verifier (prerequisite course) already guarantees at load time that callbacks terminate and only touch memory safely. But a perfectly memory-safe scheduler can still have a bad *policy*: it can forget a task in a custom DSQ forever. sched_ext adds runtime checks on top of the verifier:

- **Callback validation**: invalid return values or arguments (for example a bad DSQ id or enqueue flags) are errors that unload the scheduler.
- **`scx_bpf_error()`**: the scheduler can abort itself with a message.
- **Watchdog**: if any runnable task waits longer than `ops.timeout_ms` without running, the scheduler exits with `SCX_EXIT_ERROR_STALL`. The default and the maximum is 30 s.
- **SysRq-S**: an operator key sequence that forces the unload; SysRq-D dumps debug state without unloading.

blocks.title: Every failure path ends with tasks back on the fair class

nodes.label:
exit info + dump
to user space

scenes.caption: At load time the verifier proves memory safety and termination. A rejected program never becomes the scheduler, so nothing changes.
At run time, an invalid result (say, a bad DSQ id) or an explicit scx_bpf_error() triggers an error exit.
The watchdog catches policy bugs the verifier cannot: a task that is runnable but never picked. It reports the task name and how long it waited.
Operator or owner exits take the same road. During load, unload and error recovery the kernel runs in bypass mode with simple queues and 5 ms slices so every task makes progress.

blocks.md: How fast is a stall caught? All schedulers share one watchdog that runs every half of the timeout, and checks each CPU's runnable tasks against `runnable_at + timeout`. A task that stops being picked at time 0 becomes overdue at the timeout $T$, but the next check can come up to $T/2$ later. Ignoring jiffy rounding, detection lands between $T$ and $1.5T$. The tick also checks that the watchdog itself has run within $T$.

scenes.caption: With the default 30 s timeout, a starved task is reported between 30 and 45 s after it stopped being scheduled. Simplified model: ignores jiffy granularity.
A scheduler can set a shorter timeout_ms (never above 30 s) to fail fast in testing: 5 s gives detection within 5 to 7.5 s.

blocks.md: Ignoring kernel bugs, the scx README puts the worst case plainly: a broken sched_ext scheduler can starve some threads until the watchdog fires. It cannot corrupt memory, and the machine returns to the fair scheduler on its own.

Running one in production involves a few more realities:

- **Kernel config**: `CONFIG_SCHED_CLASS_EXT`, `CONFIG_BPF_SYSCALL`, `CONFIG_BPF_JIT` and `CONFIG_DEBUG_INFO_BTF`, among others listed in the docs.
- **No ABI stability**: callbacks, constants and `scx_bpf_*` kfuncs may change between kernel versions, so schedulers track kernels (the dispatch helper renames after 6.12 are an example).
- **Knobs are the scheduler's job**: nice is delivered through `ops.set_weight()` and cgroup `cpu.weight`, `cpu.max`, `cpu.idle` through cgroup callbacks. A scheduler may ignore them.
- **Observability**: `/sys/kernel/sched_ext/state`, `root/ops`, and the `root/events` counters (fallback CPU picks, default slice refills, bypass activations).

The [sched-ext/scx](https://github.com/sched-ext/scx) repository collects schedulers, mostly with Rust user-space parts:

- **scx_rusty**: round robin per domain (default one per LLC) in BPF, with a Rust user-space load balancer moving tasks between domains.
- **scx_lavd**: latency-criticality aware virtual deadline, motivated by gaming interactivity, with domains per LLC, core type and NUMA node.
- **scx_bpfland**: vruntime-based, all decisions in BPF, boosts tasks with many voluntary context switches as interactive.
- **scx_layered**: classifies tasks into configurable layers (for example by cgroup) with per-layer CPU guarantees.
- **scx_rustland**: makes most decisions in user-space Rust, showing that heavier logic can live outside the kernel.

Misconception: switching to a sched_ext scheduler is a free speedup. Each one encodes tradeoffs for a workload. scx_simple's own header says it suits a single uniform L3 and that its FIFO mode lets saturating threads drown out interactive ones. Benchmark your workload against the fair class, and check whether the scheduler honors the cgroup limits you rely on.

blocks.question: After switching a host to a sched_ext scheduler, a batch container's cpu.max limit is no longer enforced. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The verifier strips cgroup checks from BPF programs
cpu.max only applies to realtime tasks, which sched_ext does not handle
The kernel crashed back to bypass mode, where cgroups are ignored
cgroup CPU controls are passed to the BPF scheduler through callbacks and this scheduler does not implement them
blocks.explain: The kernel docs state the core reports cpu.max, cpu.weight and cpu.idle to the BPF scheduler via ops.cgroup_init() and cgroup_set_* callbacks, and each scheduler decides whether to implement them. Many ignore some of them, so read the scheduler's docs.

blocks.question: A scheduler with the default timeout has a bug: tasks of one cgroup are inserted into a custom DSQ that dispatch never reads. What do you observe?
options: Those tasks freeze, then within about 30 to 45 s the scheduler is unloaded with a stall error and everything runs on fair again
The machine hangs until rebooted because BPF code runs with interrupts disabled
The verifier refuses to load the scheduler because a DSQ is never consumed
The tasks run anyway because custom DSQs fall back to the global DSQ after one slice
blocks.explain: The verifier checks memory safety and termination, not whether your policy eventually runs every task. The watchdog sees runnable tasks older than 30 s on its next check (every 15 s), exits with SCX_EXIT_ERROR_STALL, and tasks revert to the fair class.

blocks.question: You are prototyping a new policy and want stalls reported in seconds, not tens of seconds. What do you change?
options: Raise SCX_SLICE_DFL so tasks run longer
Set ops.timeout_ms to a smaller value, such as 5000
Set ops.timeout_ms to 60000 so the watchdog runs more often
Enable SCX_OPS_SWITCH_PARTIAL
blocks.explain: timeout_ms sets the watchdog deadline and the check interval is half of it, so 5000 ms means detection within about 5 to 7.5 s. Values above 30000 are rejected, and slice length does not affect stall detection.
